source: Mitchell, Selman, Levesque (1992) Hard and easy distributions of SAT problems
finding: Random 3-SAT cost to a Davis-Putnam solver is easy when under-constrained (few clauses) or over-constrained (many), and hard in between. The hardest region is where about half of formulas are satisfiable.
numbers: Median recursive DP calls peak near clauses/variables = 4.3 for 50 variables. 50%-satisfiable point: 4.55 at 20 vars, 4.3 at 50 vars, 4.3 at 140 vars; conjectured about 4.25 for very large N.
limits: Small-formula boundary effect; ratio only conjectured in the limit; one simple solver; random instances, not structured ones.
agent_relevance: Difficulty of a constraint set depends on how tightly constrained it is. Code can estimate this and budget solver time, and expect UNSAT answers to be costly.

source: Mitchell, Selman, Levesque (1992) Hard and easy distributions of SAT problems
finding: Splitting the 50-variable curve into satisfiable and unsatisfiable cases shows different shapes. Rare short unsat formulas are very hard; rare long sat formulas stay moderately hard.
numbers: Figure 3: median DP calls plotted separately for sat and unsat, 50-variable random 3-SAT, against clause/variable ratio.
limits: Medians hide a heavy tail: the authors note a very small number of very large values.
agent_relevance: Proving UNSAT (no model exists, so a counterexample search fails) costs more than finding a model. A time-out must not be read as SAT.

source: Mitchell, Selman, Levesque (1992) Hard and easy distributions of SAT problems
finding: The authors argue earlier average-case SAT results looked easy because of the instance distribution (constant-probability model), so benchmark choice decides whether a solver test means anything.
numbers: Argument section on the constant-probability model versus the fixed-clause-length model; runs at 20, 50 and 140 variables.
limits: 1992 paper; basic DP with unit propagation.
agent_relevance: Any test of our scaffold's solver step must state its instance distribution. Easy instances overstate the benefit of a solver call.

source: Monasson, Zecchina, Kirkpatrick, Selman, Troyansky (1999) 2+p-SAT: typical-case complexity and the phase transition
finding: Statistical-physics analysis of K-SAT. The SAT/UNSAT change is continuous for 2-SAT-like mixes and discontinuous (random first-order) for 3-SAT. The discontinuous kind goes with exponential cost growth.
numbers: Replica-symmetric estimate for 3-SAT threshold about 4.60 versus experiments about 4.27. Experiments used 10,000 to 40,000 formulae per (N,p), N from 50 up, with TABLEAU (Davis-Putnam) and MODOC.
limits: Theory part is non-rigorous (replica method); experiments only between K=2 and K=3.
agent_relevance: Explains why some constraint sets are cheap and others not. Suggests a hard UNSAT core is a structural property, not noise.

source: Monasson et al. (1999) 2+p-SAT
finding: Friedgut's theorem gives a sharp threshold for K-SAT (SAT probability goes to 1 below, 0 above). Whether the threshold converges to a fixed limit was supported only by experiment then. The easy-hard-easy cost pattern is typical of heuristic solvers.
numbers: No new numbers; cites Friedgut.
limits: Friedgut leaves the existence of a limit open.
agent_relevance: Background for G1-style budgeting: effort is not smooth in constraint count.

source: Ding, Sly, Sun (2021) Proof of the satisfiability conjecture for large k
finding: Proves a sharp satisfiability threshold for random k-SAT for all k at least an absolute constant k0, given by an explicit one-step replica symmetry breaking formula. For k=2 the threshold is 1 (earlier result).
numbers: Threshold alpha_sat(k) explicit for k >= k0; k=2 threshold 1.
limits: Large k only; k=3 (the 4.26 case) is not proved here.
agent_relevance: The 4.26 rule of thumb for 3-SAT remains an empirical estimate; only large k is proved.

source: Moskewicz, Madigan, Zhao, Zhang, Malik (2001) Chaff: Engineering an efficient SAT solver
finding: Chaff adds two watched literals per clause for unit propagation, the VSIDS decision heuristic, and restarts that keep learned clauses. These made industrial-size SAT practical.
numbers: Over 90% of run time was boolean constraint propagation. At least 1 order of magnitude (often 2) faster than SATO and GRASP on hard EDA instances. On VLIW-SAT.1.0 Chaff finished all 100 in under 10,000 s total while SATO and GRASP aborted the first 19 of 20 tried. On another set Chaff finished all 100 within a 100 s per-instance limit in under 1,000 s.
quote: this speedup is not the result of sophisticated learning strategies
limits: Authors' own 2001 runs; GRASP was not rerun locally; the speedup is attributed to engineering, not new learning theory.
agent_relevance: Solver speed comes from cheap propagation. A solver call is a cheap deterministic check for the agent when constraints are in CNF.

source: Moskewicz et al. (2001) Chaff
finding: VSIDS counts literals in recent conflict clauses and decays the counts, so search follows where conflicts happen. Restarts clear decisions but keep learned clauses so the analysis is not repeated.
numbers: Learned-clause size limit 20 literals by default in the text; 100 in one configuration for satisfiable sets.
limits: Parameters tuned per benchmark family (option sets A and B chosen per set).
agent_relevance: Analogue of G2: revise from real failure output (conflicts), not from opinion.

source: de Moura, Bjorner (2008) Z3: An efficient SMT solver
finding: Z3 combines a DPLL-based SAT solver with a congruence-closure core and satellite theory solvers (linear arithmetic, bit-vectors, arrays, tuples) and an E-matching engine for quantifiers. It reads SMT-LIB and can supply a model.
numbers: A prototype won 4 first places and 7 second places in SMT-COMP 2007. First external release Sept 2007. Spec# switched from Simplify to Z3 in May 2007.
limits: Four-page tool paper with no benchmark table; quantified or nonlinear problems can return unknown.
agent_relevance: Most LLM-plus-solver work calls this solver. For S4/S7 it gives models (counterexamples) and unsat answers; unknown must be handled as a third outcome.

source: de Moura, Bjorner (2008) Z3
finding: Pex uses Z3 to produce new test inputs with different program behaviour, giving a small suite with maximal coverage. Spec#/Boogie uses it to prove programs or find errors.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Qualitative client description.
agent_relevance: Model-finding as test generation is the same operation as finding a counterexample model in S4.

source: Selsam, Lamm, Bunz, Liang, de Moura, Dill (2019) Learning a SAT solver from single-bit supervision (NeuroSAT)
finding: A message-passing network trained only on the one bit sat/unsat learns to predict satisfiability and, by clustering literal embeddings, to decode satisfying assignments. Training used SR(n): pairs of sat/unsat problems that differ by one negated literal.
numbers: Trained on SR(U(10,40)) with 26 iterations. Test SR(40): 85% overall accuracy, 96% on unsat, 73% on sat, satisfying assignment decoded for 70% of satisfiable problems. SR(200): 25% solved with 4x the training iterations, under 10% at the training count. On 4,888 satisfiable problems from other domains, assignments decoded for 85% (512 iterations).
limits: Far weaker than CDCL; small problems; answers are checkable but not guaranteed.
agent_relevance: A decoded assignment can be verified by code for free. A guess is not proof, but the check is.

source: Selsam et al. (2019) NeuroSAT
finding: A variant trained on unsat data (NeuroUNSAT) finds unsat-core literals: core literals end up in their own cluster.
numbers: Predicts satisfiability on its test set with 100% accuracy in that variant; core literals cluster together 98% of the time.
limits: Applies to its own SR(n) test distribution.
agent_relevance: An unsat core (a smallest conflicting subset) is the useful output for G2: it locates the failing constraint.

source: Ye, Chen, Dillig, Durrett (2023) SatLM: Satisfiability-aided language models using declarative prompting
finding: The LLM writes a declarative constraint specification and Z3 solves it. This beat the same model writing an imperative program (PROGLM) and chain of thought on constraint-heavy tasks.
numbers: code-davinci-002, greedy: GSM-SYS 69.4 (SATLM) vs 43.4 (PROGLM) vs 46.5 (CoT); LSAT 35.0 vs 23.5 CoT; BoardgameQA 79.4 vs 60.7 CoT; CLUTRR 68.3 vs 58.9 PROGLM; ProofWriter 99.7 vs 83.7 PROGLM; GSM 71.8 vs 72.7 PROGLM. Self-consistency: GSM-SYS 80.9, GSM 84.8, LSAT 37.4, BoardgameQA 80.7, ProofWriter 99.7.
limits: Old model; no gain on plain GSM (71.8 vs 72.7); correctness holds only relative to the parsed spec.
agent_relevance: Core design for S4/S7: model parses, code solves. Gains concentrate where search or planning is needed, not forward arithmetic.

source: Ye et al. (2023) SatLM
finding: New state of the art on LSAT and BoardgameQA, beating models trained on the full training sets.
numbers: LSAT 30.9% (Zhong et al. 2022) to 37.4%; BoardgameQA 73.9% (Kazemi et al. 2023) to 80.7%.
limits: LSAT test set is 230 examples; only 5 samples used there for cost.
agent_relevance: Small test sets; gains of 2 to 7 points need caution.

source: Ye et al. (2023) SatLM
finding: Ablation: asking the model to predict from the spec without a real solver is only on par with standard prompting. Errors of a chain-of-thought solver are mostly planning errors.
numbers: In 40 cases where Z3 was right and the CoT solver wrong: planning errors 72.5% (GSM-SYS), 42.5% (GSM), 47.5% (CLUTRR); execution errors 27.5%, 57.5%, 52.5%.
limits: Manual analysis of 40 cases.
agent_relevance: The solver itself is what pays; a spec without a solver gives nothing (supports G7).

source: Ye et al. (2023) SatLM
finding: A declarative spec is easier to write than a plan. Accuracy on answered items is higher when the system abstains on unparsable or inconsistent specs.
numbers: GSM-SYS selective accuracy 77% vs 45% (PROGLM) at lower coverage.
limits: Coverage drops, which conflicts with G6 if abstaining on the first pass.
agent_relevance: Treat an unparsable or unsat spec as a signal, but still submit a best attempt (G6).

source: Pan, Albalak, Wang, Wang (2023) Logic-LM: Empowering LLMs with symbolic solvers for faithful logical reasoning
finding: Translate the problem to a formal language, solve with a symbolic solver (Z3 for analytical-reasoning problems such as AR-LSAT and LogicalDeduction), and self-refine on solver errors.
numbers: GPT-3.5: average +39.2% over standard prompting and +18.4% over CoT. GPT-4: +24.98% over standard, +10.44% over CoT. GPT-4 executable rate without refinement: FOLIO 79.9%, AR-LSAT 32.6%; with refinement 85.8% and 39.8%. GPT-3.5 AR-LSAT executable 11.3% to 21.8% with refinement.
limits: Five datasets; ProntoQA and ProofWriter gains are small as CoT is already strong; AR-LSAT low because translation fails.
agent_relevance: Translation failure, not solving, is the bottleneck. Solver error messages are good feedback for G2.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM
finding: Gain over CoT is largest on tasks that need hypothesizing, conditioning and search, and grows with reasoning depth.
numbers: Gain over CoT: FOLIO +21.85%, LogicalDeduction +45.67%, AR-LSAT +24.14%. By ProofWriter depth, Logic-LM beats CoT by 7.1, 5.0, 12.7, 20.0, 39.4 points at depths 0,1,2,4,5. For GPT-4 vs CoT gains on some sets are small and one is negative (-3.2%).
limits: Gains vary by dataset and model.
agent_relevance: Deep chains and constraint search benefit most; shallow ones do not need a solver.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC: neurosymbolic logical reasoning with FOL provers
finding: The LLM translates premises to first-order logic; Prover9 decides; majority vote over samples. It beats Scratchpad (same formulas, model's own verdict) and CoT.
numbers: FOLIO: StarCoder+ LINC 56.0% vs CoT 41.8% (+14.2); GPT-3.5 LINC 62.6% vs 54.9% CoT. Abstract: StarCoder+ with LINC beats GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 with CoT by absolute 38% and 10%; GPT-4 with LINC is 26% above CoT on ProofWriter and comparable on FOLIO.
limits: Prover9 (first-order), not SMT; FOLIO subset of 182 examples; GPT-4 on FOLIO shows no gain.
agent_relevance: Scratchpad (formal text but no solver) does not help: the prover call is the active ingredient.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC
finding: Translation errors: formulas contain syntax errors, most often one symbol used with several arities. CoT often concludes something different from what its reasoning suggests.
numbers: Syntax-error rate 38% StarCoder+, 24% GPT-3.5, 13% GPT-4.
limits: From analysis of generations on FOLIO.
agent_relevance: Parse-check formulas in code and reject ill-formed ones before solving.

source: Wei, Wu, Wan, Zhou, Suresh, Tan, Aiken, Koyejo, Wang (2025) SATBench
finding: 2,100 puzzles from SAT formulas turned into stories by an LLM; difficulty by clause count (easy 4-19, medium 20-30, hard 31-50). Task: say SAT or UNSAT, zero-shot.
numbers: o4-mini overall 89.3%, DeepSeek-R1 87.8%, DeepSeek-V3 84.0%, Claude-3.7-Sonnet 74.8%, gpt-4o 58.0%, LLaMA3.1-8B 38.2%. Average over models: easy 78.5, medium 59.8, hard 53.0 (random baseline 50). o4-mini on hard 78.0%.
limits: Narrative framing adds difficulty over raw CNF; human validation passing rates above 90% on a subset; random baseline 50%.
agent_relevance: Pure prompting is near chance for large constraint sets, so S4 should call a solver, not ask the model.

source: Wei et al. (2025) SATBench
finding: Models do much better on SAT than UNSAT at hard size: they favour answering satisfiable. The largest error type is satisfiability bias (claim SAT with an invalid assignment).
numbers: Average on hard: SAT 66.7% vs UNSAT 39.3%. o4-mini hard UNSAT 65.0%. Error mix o4-mini: satisfiability bias 68.7%, context inconsistency 17.0%, condition omission 14.3%, spurious priors 0.0%; DeepSeek-R1: 40.5%, 44.7%, 12.6%, 2.1%.
limits: Qualitative classification of wrong predictions.
agent_relevance: The G3 hazard: a claimed model must be checked by code against every clause before it counts as a pass.

source: Wei et al. (2025) SATBench
finding: Right answer, weaker trace: reasoning-trace accuracy is lower than prediction accuracy, especially on SAT.
numbers: Prediction/trace accuracy: o4-mini SAT 94.7/74.6, UNSAT 83.6/74.1; DeepSeek-R1 SAT 85.2/73.8, UNSAT 90.3/82.1; Claude-3.7 SAT 83.2/47.4.
limits: Traces were judged by a model-based checker, which has its own errors.
agent_relevance: Supports that written reasoning is not a reliable record of how the answer was reached (schema section 1).

source: Wei et al. (2025) SATBench
finding: Text framing costs accuracy: the same formulas as raw CNF are easier. Error-aware prompts fix many failures; LoRA fine-tuning on checked traces helps little.
numbers: Puzzle vs formula accuracy: gpt-4o-mini 53.6 vs 54.8; gpt-4o 58.2 vs 59.2; DeepSeek-V3 84.0 vs 87.3; o4-mini 89.4 vs 94.3. Error-aware prompts corrected 60.4% (o4-mini) and 73.2% (R1) of earlier failures. LoRA on 1,100 o4-mini traces: Qwen2.5-14B 51.9% to 53.6%.
limits: Prompt fix was tested on previously failed cases only (selection effect); no fresh held-out run.
agent_relevance: Translate to formal form first (as SatLM) rather than reason in story text.

source: Lin, Le Bras, Richardson et al. (2025) ZebraLogic
finding: Zebra grid puzzles as constraint satisfaction with a unique solution. Accuracy collapses as search space and Z3 conflicts grow (the 'curse of complexity'), even for large models.
numbers: Overall: o1 81.0%, DeepSeek-R1 78.7%, o1-preview 71.4%, o1-mini 59.7%, Claude Sonnet 3.5 36.2%, Llama-3.1-405B 32.6%. Llama-405B: medium 22.5%, large 1.5%, x-large 0.0%. Sonnet 3.5 large 4.0%, x-large 1.0%. o1-preview x-large 17.0%.
limits: Unique-solution puzzles (no UNSAT cases); grids up to 6x6.
agent_relevance: Solver conflict count predicts when the model alone will fail.

source: Lin et al. (2025) ZebraLogic
finding: Difficulty measured two ways: search-space size (small up to x-large at or above 10^10) and average Z3 conflicts over 32 runs. Zero conflicts means forward chaining suffices.
numbers: Size classes: medium 10^3 to 10^6, large 10^6 to 10^10, x-large 10^10 and above.
limits: Z3 conflict counts depend on solver heuristics.
agent_relevance: A cheap proxy for hardness before spending tokens.

source: Wu, Barrett, Narodytska (2024) Lemur: integrating LLMs in automated program verification
finding: The LLM proposes loop invariants; an automated verifier checks them and returns feedback. A calculus with a soundness proof.
numbers: Code2Inv (133 benchmarks): ESBMC alone 68, Code2Inv 92, Lemur(GPT-3.5) 103, Lemur(GPT-4) 107 solved. 47 SV-COMP benchmarks: UAutomizer 1, ESBMC 1, Lemur(GPT-3.5) 14, Lemur(GPT-4) 25. Average proposals per solved instance 4.7 to 8.6.
limits: Small benchmark sets; specific GPT versions of 2023.
agent_relevance: Propose-then-check with a sound checker: an LLM guess is never trusted until a solver confirms (G3).

source: Kirtania, Gupta, Radhakrishna (2024) Logic-LM++: multi-step refinement for symbolic formulations
finding: Refinement of Logic-LM: the LLM compares two candidate formulations pairwise and a backtracking agent rejects edits that change meaning. Plain self-refinement can make a formula worse.
numbers: Abstract: improves 18.5% over standard prompting, 12.3% over CoT, 5% over Logic-LM (GPT-4). FOLIO test set 204 examples.
limits: Relies on LLM pairwise judgments, which G5 distrusts.
agent_relevance: Accept a formula edit only if code checks it against solver output; unanchored refinement can drift.
